title: Race and skin colour
def: The Quran makes colour and language signs of God’s creation, and no ground of superiority (49:13, 30:22).
what: “Among His signs is the creation of the heavens and the earth and the difference of your languages and colours” (30:22). “O mankind, We created you from a male and a female and made you peoples and tribes that you may know one another; the noblest of you with God is the most pious” (49:13). The Prophet said that no Arab is superior to a non-Arab, nor a white to a black, except by piety (Ahmad).
misread: That Muhammad was black, or that Islam is only for Arabs.
sources: Muhammad was Arab, of Quraysh; the claim that he was black has no historical basis. The first muezzin, Bilal, was an Ethiopian former slave, and the Prophet rebuked Abu Dharr for insulting a man by his mother’s blackness, saying “you are a man in whom there is ignorance” (Sahih al-Bukhari). Muslim societies have also known racism, and the teaching is a standard against which they are judged.

title: Rass, People of the
def: A people named twice in the Quran as destroyed after rejecting their prophet; who they were is not known.
what: The Quran mentions “the companions of the Rass” with Noah’s people and Thamud and ʿĀd (25:38, 50:12). Rass means a well or pit. Commentators suggest different peoples and places, and none is certain.

title: Reason and faith
def: Islam does not call for blind belief; the Quran calls on people to reflect, reason and examine claims.
what: The Quran asks: “Will they not reflect?” (47:24), “Do they not ponder?” (4:82), and says “bring your proof if you are truthful” (2:111). It uses the word for “reason” in many forms in about fifty places. Classical scholars from the Mu’tazilites to al-Ghazali and Averroes argued for reason in different ways, and the philosopher Ibn Rushd wrote that the study of nature is commanded by scripture.
sources: Schools differ on how much reason can establish apart from revelation. The Muslim position is that revelation and sound reason do not contradict, and that when they appear to, one of them has been misread.

title: Riba
def: Usury: gain taken from a loan at the borrower’s expense, which the Quran forbids.
what: The Quran says that God has permitted trade and forbidden ribā (2:275), and warns of a war from God against those who continue it (2:278–279). It adds that if the debtor is in difficulty, there should be time for him, and that to forgive the debt is better (2:280). A hadith in Sahih Muslim says the Prophet cursed the one who takes it, the one who gives it, the one who records it and the two who witness it.
Muslims have developed finance on other principles, such as profit-sharing, sale at an agreed mark-up and leasing.
misread: That Islam is simply against business.
sources: The same teaching is found in the other scriptures: the Torah forbids charging interest to the poor (Exodus 22:25), and the medieval Church banned usury for centuries. Islam is a religion in which trade is praised, and the Prophet was himself a merchant. The prohibition is aimed at gain from the weakness of a debtor, and not at commerce.

title: Rabb
def: A divine name: the loving Lord and commanding Master, used in the forms Rabbī (my Lord) and Rabbanā (our Lord) when calling on God.
what: Rabb is the Arabic word for Lord. It combines the sense of one who nurtures and sustains with the sense of one who has authority and commands. It is a divine name, and the Quran opens with praise to God as Rabb al-ʿālamīn, Lord of the worlds (1:2). Muslims use it in the possessive forms Rabbī, my Lord, and Rabbanā, our Lord, when they call on God in supplication. Many of the prayers recorded in the Quran begin with it, such as “Our Lord, give us good in this world and good in the world to come” (2:201).
misread: That “Lord” alone gives the meaning, when rabb joins loving care with command.

title: Rabbana Hab Lana min Azwajina
ar: ربنا هب لنا من أزواجنا وذرياتنا قرة أعين واجعلنا للمتقين إماما
tr: Rabbanā Hab Lanā min Azwājinā wa Dhurriyyātinā Qurrata Aʿyunin wa Ijʿalnā lil-Muttaqīna Imāman
def: “Our Lord, grant that our spouses and children be a joy to us, and make us leaders of the God-fearing”; said when speaking of spouses or children.
what: This is a supplication from the Quran, in which believers ask God for spouses and offspring who will be a comfort to the eyes, a joy and a source of pride, and for the grace to be leaders of the muttaqīn, those mindful of God. It appears at 25:74 in the description of the servants of the Most Merciful. Muslims say it in any conversation about wives, husbands or children, and parents recite it as a prayer for their family, asking that those closest to them be pious and that they themselves be an example to others.

faruqi.term: RABBANĀ HAB LANĀ MIN AZWĀJINĀ WA DHURRIYYATINĀ QURRATA A‘YUNIN WA IJA‘ALNĀ LIL MUTTAQĪNA IMĀMAN.

title: Rabbi Ishrah li Sadri
ar: رب اشرح لي صدري ويسر لي أمري واحلل عقدة من لساني يفقهوا قولي
tr: Rabbi Ishraḥ lī Ṣadrī wa Yassir lī Amrī wa Uḥlul ʿUqdatan min Lisānī Yafqahū Qawlī
def: “My Lord, expand my chest and ease my task; loosen the knot in my tongue so that they understand my speech”; said at the opening of a speech.
what: This is the prayer of the Prophet Moses (peace be upon him) when God sent him to Pharaoh, recorded in the Quran (20:25-28). He asked for his chest to be opened with confidence, for his task to be made easy, and for the knot in his tongue to be untied so that people would understand what he said. Muslims recite it at the start of a speech, a lecture or a sermon, and before an exam or a task that calls for clear speech. It asks God for clarity of mind and expression and for ease in the work, and it recalls that a prophet himself sought God’s help before addressing others.

faruqi.term: RABBI ISHRAḤ LĪ ṢADRĪ WA YASSIR LĪ AMRĪ WA UḤLUL ‘UQDATAN MIN LISĀNĪ YAFQAHU QAWLĪ.

title: Radiya
def: To be pleased; used of God’s pleasure with His servants and theirs with Him.
what: Raḍiya is an Arabic verb meaning to be pleased or satisfied. It is used in the Quran of God’s pleasure with those who believe and do good, and of their pleasure with Him: God is well pleased with them, and they are well pleased with Him (98:8). The verb gives the nouns riḍā, pleasure, and riḍwān, a state of pleasure that God grants. It also gives the invocation raḍiya Allāhu ʿanhu, “may God be pleased with him”, said after the name of a Companion. Seeking God’s pleasure is a stated aim of the believer’s conduct and worship.

title: Radiya Allahu 'Anhu
ar: رضي الله عنه / رضي الله عنهم
def: “May God be pleased with him (or with them).” It is said whenever a Companion of the Prophet is mentioned by name.
what: Raḍiya Allāhu ʿanhu means “may God be pleased with him”. For a woman the form is ʿanhā, and for several people ʿanhum. Muslims say it after the name of a Companion of the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him), and in writing it is often abbreviated to RA. It rests on the Quran’s praise of the first Emigrants and Helpers, “God is well pleased with them, and they are well pleased with Him” (9:100), and on God’s pleasure with the believers who pledged allegiance under the tree (48:18). It expresses love and respect for the generation that carried the message to later Muslims.

title: Rahim, al-
def: A divine name: the One who is always merciful.
what: Al-Raḥīm is a divine name meaning the One who is constantly merciful. It comes from the same root as al-Raḥmān, and the two stand together in the opening phrase of every chapter of the Quran but one: bismillāh al-Raḥmān al-Raḥīm (1:1). Where al-Raḥmān is usually read as describing the breadth of God’s mercy, al-Raḥīm is read as describing its constancy toward those who believe and turn to Him. Muslims say the phrase at the beginning of their acts, and use the name in prayer to ask for His mercy.
misread: That God is only a stern judge, when His mercy is stated at the head of the Quran.

title: Rahima
def: With its derivatives, to consider or act with sympathy and mercy.
what: Raḥima is an Arabic verb meaning to show sympathy and mercy, in thought and in action. Its derivatives include raḥmah, mercy, the divine names al-Raḥmān and al-Raḥīm, and raḥim, which also names the womb and the bond of kinship. The Quran says that God’s mercy encompasses all things (7:156), and describes the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) as sent as a mercy to the worlds (21:107). The verb is also used in a prayer for the dead, “may God have mercy on him”, and believers are told to show mercy to one another.
misread: That mercy is only a feeling, when the root joins feeling with action.

title: Rahmah Allah 'Alayh
ar: رحمة الله عليه / رحمة الله عليها / رحمة الله عليهم
def: “May God’s mercy be upon him (her or them).” It is said whenever a departed Muslim is mentioned by name.
what: Raḥmah Allāh ʿalayh means “may God’s mercy be upon him”. The form for a woman is ʿalayhā, and for several people ʿalayhim. Muslims say it after the name of a Muslim who has died, as a prayer that God will have mercy on him. It is closely related to the phrase raḥimahu Allāh, “may God have mercy on him”, with the same meaning. Said in conversation, in a sermon or when the name of an earlier scholar is cited, it keeps the dead in the prayers of the living and expresses the respect the community owes to those who came before.

title: Rahman, al-
def: A divine name: the Merciful, whose mercy embraces all creation.
what: Al-Raḥmān is a divine name meaning the Merciful. It is used only of God. The Quran gives it as an alternative to the name Allah: “Call upon God or call upon the Most Merciful; by whichever you call, His are the best names” (17:110). It stands beside al-Raḥīm in the phrase that begins nearly every chapter. A whole chapter, al-Raḥmān (chapter 55), opens with the name and lists the favours of God to people and jinn. Muslims often read the name as pointing to the all-embracing scope of God’s mercy, which reaches every creature in this life.
misread: That God is chiefly a God of wrath, when His most frequent name is Merciful.

title: Raka'a
def: To bow in worship, as required in Islamic worship; the root of rukūʿ and rakʿah.
what: Rakaʿa is the Arabic verb for bowing in worship. In the salah it names the act of bending from the standing position, with the hands resting on the knees, while saying words of praise to God. The same root gives rukūʿ and rakʿah. The Quran commands believers to establish the prayer, give zakah and bow with those who bow (2:43). It also tells them to bow and prostrate themselves and worship their Lord (22:77). Faruqi renders the word as kneeling, though the act in the prayer is a bow, and the sense is humble submission before God.
misread: That it means kneeling, when the movement in the salah is a bow from standing.

title: Rasm al-Qur'ani, al-
def: The calligraphy and orthography of the written Quran.
what: Al-Rasm al-Qurʾānī is the Quranic script: the way the text of the Quran is written down, in its calligraphy and its spelling. It records the spellings used in the copies of the Quran made under the third caliph, Uthman ibn Affan (may God be pleased with him), and so is also called al-rasm al-ʿUthmānī. Scholars have long studied it, and the scribes who copied the Quran have kept to it with great care. Some spellings differ from those of ordinary Arabic writing, and they are preserved as they were first set down. The study has its own books and experts, who also treat the marks added later to guide reading.
misread: That it is ordinary Arabic spelling, when it preserves a specific written tradition of the text.

title: Rasul
def: Nouns from one root for a person devoted to al-risālah, the commission to convey God’s message.
what: Rasūl and mursal both come from the root of risālah. A rasūl is one sent with a message, and a mursal is one who has been sent. In the Quran the words denote a messenger of God, a person devoted to the commission of conveying His message. The Quran names many messengers and says that a messenger was sent to every community (16:36). It calls Muhammad (peace be upon him) the Messenger of God and the seal of the prophets (33:40). In the common usage of scholars, every rasūl is a nabiyy, and the term often points to those who brought a scripture or a law.
misread: That “messenger” means a postman, when it denotes someone commissioned by God with a revelation.

title: Rasul, al-
def: The title of Muhammad (peace be upon him), the Prophet; “the Messenger”.
what: Al-Rasūl, with the article, is the name by which the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) is known in the Quran, “the Messenger”. The Quran uses it when it commands believers to obey God and obey the Messenger (4:59), and it appears in the declaration of faith, that Muhammad is the Messenger of God. In Islamic usage, the word with the article means him in particular among all messengers. Muslims follow what he taught and showed in his life, which is preserved in the Sunnah, and love and respect for him is part of their faith. His name is followed by the invocation of peace whenever it is mentioned.

title: Ra'uf, al-
def: A divine name: the One who is deeply and sympathetically concerned with the lot of human beings.
what: Al-Raʾūf is a divine name meaning the One who shows deep, tender concern for His creatures. It points to a sympathy that attends to the situation of people and does not leave them in hardship. The Quran joins it often with al-Raḥīm. The Quran says that God is full of kindness (raʾūf) and mercy toward people (2:143). It also uses the same word of the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him), who is described as compassionate and merciful toward the believers (9:128). Muslims call on the name when asking God for gentleness and relief.

title: Raziq, al-
def: A divine name: the One who grants rizq, the sustenance every creature needs.
what: Al-Rāziq is a divine name meaning the One who grants rizq, what God provides for His creatures. It is a name of the provider who gives food, health and the means of living. A stronger form, al-Razzāq, the constant Provider, is the one named in the Quran (51:58). The Quran teaches that no creature on earth lacks its provision from God (11:6). Muslims therefore thank Him for what they receive, work lawfully to earn it, and trust that they will be given what is written for them. The name is cited in supplications asking for lawful provision.

title: Rida, al-
def: The pleasure of God, which believers seek; the noun from raḍiya.
what: Al-Riḍā is the pleasure of God with His servants. It is the noun from the verb raḍiya, to be pleased. The Quran speaks of God’s pleasure with the believers (98:8), and says that His pleasure (riḍwān) is greater than any other reward in Paradise (9:72). Seeking riḍā is a central aim of the believer. It is also used of a person who is content with God’s decree. Muslims pray that God be pleased with them, and the invocation said for the Companions and other righteous people asks for exactly this.

title: Rijal al-Hadith
def: The science that studies the narrators of hadith, in so far as they are narrators.
what: Rijāl al-ḥadīth means the men, and women, of hadith: the people through whom reports reached later generations. The science studies their lives and their characters as narrators: when and where they lived, whom they met and from whom they heard, and whether they were honest, accurate and trusted. Scholars collected this information into biographical dictionaries, and the judgments recorded there (jarḥ and taʿdīl, criticism and commendation) are used to assess a chain of narrators. The science treats each narrator only as a narrator, and it is one of the main tools by which a hadith is judged sound or weak.
misread: That hadith scholars accepted reports without checking the people who passed them on.

title: Rijs
def: An evil deed, or a thing that God has prohibited.
what: Rijs is an Arabic word for a filthy or abominable thing, whether a wicked act or something God has forbidden. The Quran uses it of intoxicants, gambling, idol-stones and divining arrows, which it calls an rijs from the work of Satan and which believers are told to avoid (5:90). It also tells believers to avoid the rijs of idols (22:30). The word carries a sense of moral uncleanness, which is why it is applied to what harms the soul and the community. Muslims use it for what God has declared forbidden and corrupting.
misread: That it means only physical dirt, when it extends to forbidden and corrupting acts.

title: Risalah, al-
def: God’s commissioning of a human being to convey and exemplify His message, and the life lived in loyalty to that task.
what: Al-Risālah is the message that God entrusts to a human being, together with the commission to carry it. The one commissioned must convey the message and also exemplify it by his own life. It is the office of the messenger (rasūl) and the content that he delivers. The word is also used for the life lived in constant awareness of that purpose and in loyalty to it. The Quran quotes the prophets as saying that they convey the messages of their Lord (7:62), and it commands the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) to deliver what was sent down to him (5:67). Muslims speak of the Muslim community as having its own risālah, to bear witness to the truth.
misread: That it means simply a letter or a note, when it denotes a divine commission.

title: Riwayah al-Hadith
def: The transmission of hadith: the reporting of the words, deeds, descriptions and attitudes of the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him).
what: Riwāyah al-ḥadīth is the reporting of hadith. It covers the words of the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him), his actions, his description and character, and his approval or disapproval of what others said and did. The science of riwāyah deals with the exact transmission of these reports and the care owed to their wording. The narrators passed the reports on by hearing and reading them back to their teachers, each naming the person from whom he heard. The word is often set beside dirāyah, the study of the meaning and the rules of hadith. Together they form the work that scholars used to preserve the Sunnah.

title: Rizq
def: What God grants a person out of His material bounty: sustenance, provision and livelihood.
what: Rizq is what God provides to His creatures from His bounty: food, wealth, health and all that sustains life. In Islamic teaching it comes from God, who is the Provider, while a person is still told to work to earn it. The Quran says that no creature moves on the earth without its provision resting with God (11:6), and describes Him as the Provider, firm in strength (51:58). The Quran also asks believers to spend from the rizq that God has given them, so that wealth is a trust and a means of doing good.
misread: That it is only money or income, when it covers every provision that God grants.

title: Ruku'
def: The bow in the salah; a single unit of the prayer, with its bow, is a rakʿah.
what: Rukūʿ is the bow in the salah, made by bending from the standing position with the hands on the knees while praising God. Faruqi renders it as kneeling or genuflection. The singular rakʿah names one complete unit of the prayer, which contains one bow and two prostrations. The Quran commands believers to bow with those who bow (2:43) and to bow and prostrate themselves and worship their Lord (22:77). The word has given the prayer its units, and Muslims count their prayers by the number of rakʿāt. In the bow a worshipper declares the glory of his Lord, the Almighty.
misread: That rukūʿ is kneeling, when it is a bow made from standing.
